copy.headline: Your eggs have 5 weeks. Not 5 days.
copy.body: The number printed on the carton is not telling you what you think it is.

copy.heroNumberCaption: How long eggs keep in the refrigerator after you bring them home.
copy.citation: USDA FSIS, Shell Eggs from Farm to Table

copy.headline: Two dates. Only one is about you.
items: Sell-By or EXP. A stocking instruction written for the store, not a safety cutoff written for you.
Pack date. The day the eggs were graded and boxed. This is the one your fridge clock actually starts from.

copy.headline: How to read the carton
items: Find the three-digit code stamped near the date.
That is the pack date, counted from January 1.
Add three to five weeks. That is your real window.

copy.headline: When you are unsure, ask the egg
items: Fill a bowl with cold water.
copy.citation: The float test measures the air cell, which grows as an egg ages.

copy.headline: Roughly three in four people throw eggs out on the date alone.
copy.body: Not because the eggs went bad. Because nobody ever told them the date was a stocking guideline.

copy.headline: Keep this. Your egg week-by-week.
copy.body: Hard-boiling gets easier as eggs age. Older eggs peel cleaner than fresh ones.

copy.headline: Your fridge is full of food with more time than you think.
copy.ctaLine: fond tracks the real window on everything you buy, so you stop guessing at labels.
